events.title: Tertullian's Apologeticum
events.summary: Writing at Carthage in 197, the year of the Severan civil war, Tertullian addressed to the provincial governors a legal and rhetorical defence of Christians, attacking trials for "the name" alone and claiming that Christians prayed for the emperor; it contains his famous "semen est sanguis Christianorum" and marks the birth of Latin Christian literature.

events.title: Kartir's inscriptions and the Zoroastrian state church
events.summary: Under Bahram II the high priest Kartir carved inscriptions boasting that he had established fire temples across the empire and in conquered Roman lands and struck down Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Nazarenes, Christians and Manichaeans; they document the formation of a Zoroastrian orthodoxy that later shaped Persian treatment of Christians.
events.debate: Date c. 280-293; the scale of persecution claimed is debated.

events.title: Constantine restricts unilateral divorce
events.summary: A law of 331 (CTh 3.16.1) allowed a wife to repudiate her husband only if he was a murderer, poisoner or tomb violator, and a husband his wife only for adultery, poisoning or procuring, with severe property penalties otherwise, a sharp break with the classical freedom of divorce often attributed to Christian influence.
events.debate: Christian versus traditional moral motives for Constantine's family legislation are debated (Evans Grubbs).

events.title: Creation of the defensor civitatis
events.summary: Valentinian I instructed the prefect Probus to appoint in each city of Illyricum a "defender of the plebs" to protect the humble against the powerful (CTh 1.29.1, 368 or 364), giving them summary jurisdiction in small cases; the office spread to the whole empire and later passed largely to bishops.

events.title: Valentinian makes infanticide a capital crime
events.summary: A law of Valentinian, Valens and Gratian of 374 (CTh 9.14.1) declared the killing of an infant punishable by death; a contemporary law (CTh 9.14.1 and CJ 8.51.2) also restricted exposure, though the sale and exposure of newborns continued, as later legislation shows.

events.title: Gratian moves the western court from Trier to Milan
events.summary: After 378 Gratian spent more time in the Danube and Italian theatres and by 381 had settled at Milan, close to Ambrose, whose influence on him grew; Trier ceased to be the main western residence, and the Gallic army, feeling neglected, backed Magnus Maximus in 383.
